case.case_title: Dona Diana Pearly v. Premaratne, Acting Secretary Educational Service Board and Another
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 790/96, decided on 16 June 1997

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s fundamental right under Article 12(1) was infringed by the failure to appoint her as an Assistant English Teacher after successfully completing the DELIC course, due to a correction of an error in her examination marks.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that having been admitted to and successfully completed the DELIC course based on the originally disclosed marks, she was entitled to appointment as an English teacher, and refusal of appointment violated Article 12(1). Alternatively, that successful completion of the course was the sole criterion for appointment.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that merit as determined by the competitive examination marks remained relevant for appointment, and the petitioner was not qualified once the error was corrected. The correction of the error and consequent refusal of appointment did not deny equal protection. Also, any delay in correcting the error was not a violation and the remedy was elsewhere.
key_facts: Petitioner scored 53 out of 100 marks initially, making her eligible for the DELIC course.
Later it was discovered her marks were actually 53 out of 200, changing her merit ranking from 126 to 2403.
Petitioner was allowed to complete the DELIC course and passed the final exam.
There was an unreasonable delay of over eight months in correcting the error and informing the petitioner of its effect on her eligibility.
Some colleagues received appointments while petitioner did not.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that Article 12(1) guarantees equal protection of the law, which requires that administrative processes be conducted fairly and expeditiously. While correcting an error in marks does not itself breach equality, the unreasonable delay and failure to inform the petitioner promptly constituted a denial of equal protection.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The court found that the delay of over eight months in correcting the error and over a year in informing the petitioner of its effect was not necessary or usual, showing lack of concern for her rights. This delay caused avoidable prejudice and denied her equal protection under the law.
principles_established: Correction of administrative errors must be done promptly to avoid prejudice.
Equal protection includes timely and fair treatment in public recruitment processes.
Delay and failure to inform affected candidates can constitute denial of equal protection.

outcome.holding: The court held that the petitioner’s fundamental right to equal protection under Article 12(1) was infringed due to the unreasonable delay and failure to inform her of the effect of the correction. The petitioner was awarded Rs. 25,000 as compensation and costs.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Payment of Rs. 25,000 as compensation and costs to the petitioner.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the court’s reasoning as it protects against unfair administrative delay and denial of information that prejudices a candidate’s rights in public service appointments, which was the core issue in this case.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court found that the delay of over eight months in correcting the error and the failure for over a year to inform the petitioner of its effect displayed a lack of concern for her rights constituting a denial of equal protection of the law.
